speaker: nana
lines: Oh, there you are! Come here and let me look at you. That long road's worn you thin.
I'm sorry, love, you've come at a bad time. The radio's gone quiet. The set up at the mast on Brindle Peak has run out of power, and nobody can get through.
Bram, who looks after the woodstore by the big pine, keeps spare batteries. Would you fetch them for me?
And take my old camera with you. Edda, who keeps the set up there, has been wanting one for ages. She'll tell you why.

choices.text: can't the radio wait a bit?

speaker: nana
lines: Not really, love. The snow's come early this year, and once it settles in, the road closes behind it.
The radio's how we all keep an eye on each other up here. Who's short of flour, whether the lake ice is holding, whose chimney's stopped smoking.
Edda's been sitting up there with a dead set ever since it went. She won't say so, but she'll be lonely.
I'd go up myself, but these knees have done that climb for sixty winters, and they've told me they're finished with it.

speaker: nana
lines: He'll want you to do something for him first. He always does, bless him. Once you've got them, bring the batteries back here to me.

speaker: nana
lines: No batteries yet? Oh, don't worry, there's plenty of day left.
Bram keeps them in his woodstore, over by the big pine.
He's fussy, but he isn't unkind. Whatever he asks you to do, it'll be quick, and he'll be particular about it.
Bring them back here before you head up the hill, mind. There are a few things I'll need to tell you.

speaker: nana
lines: You got them off him! Heavy, aren't they? That's the radio's voice you're carrying in there.
Here, take my lantern as well. There are lantern posts all the way up the trail, so light them as you go past.
Once they're lit, they'll show you the way back down to me.
Edda keeps the set at the mast. Make sure you give these to her and nobody else.

speaker: nana
lines: Edda's an owl. She's proud, and she's kind, and she can't stand anyone making a fuss of her.
The two of us have talked on that radio every evening for thirty years.
She'll ask you whether I'm keeping well. Tell her yes. And she'll pretend she wasn't worried about me.

speaker: nana
lines: Take the climb slowly. The wind up on the ridge will have the feathers off you if you let it.
And when it's all done, come back down to me. I want to hear all about it from you.

speaker: nana
lines: Still here, love? Edda's waiting up at the mast for those batteries.
Go up through Windscar Ridge and light the posts as you pass. Go on, off you go.

speaker: nana
lines: A letter, for me? From Pell, the postmaster, all the way across the valley?
'The blue house, road head.' Well, that's me. I painted it again in the autumn so there'd be no mistaking it.
Oh. Oh, I'll need to read this one again. And probably again after that.
This is staying by the stove. Next time you're in the hamlet, would you tell Pell it found the right door? He worries.

speaker: nana
lines: There you are! I heard you on the radio, love. The whole valley heard you.

speaker: nana
lines: Edda says you did her looking for her. She sounded twenty years younger, I'm telling you.
Now, tell me one thing. Just the one, tonight. I'll get the rest out of you in the morning.

choices.text: bram's pile came to four hundred and eighty-one.
the sky went green over the peak.

speaker: nana
lines: Oh, I know. He told the whole valley on the radio, and then he told them all again.
He'll count it twice tonight, I expect. But it's the first time in years he'll like the answer.

speaker: nana
lines: The northern lights? Of course. Edda never could see the green, you know. Now at least she knows it's there.
Was it as bright as they say? No, don't tell me. I'd rather picture it myself.

speaker: nana
lines: But for tonight, come and sit out here with me for a minute. I'd like to look at those posts.
And Pip? I'm glad it was you who went up.

speaker: nana
lines: Sit down for a minute and get yourself warm. Whatever's out there will keep.
There's always a cup in this house for you. You know where they live.
Off you go whenever you're ready. The valley's still there for you to walk.

speaker: hollis
lines: I've lost a mitten. The left one, and it was the good one, too.
And I know who took it. Fen, the owl who sits watching from the pines.
Go and ask him what he's got to say for himself.

choices.text: why would an owl take a mitten?

speaker: hollis
lines: He's an owl, isn't he? He sits up there and watches everybody with those great big eyes.
And he never says a word to anyone. Looks guilty to me.
He sits in the pines, over on the creek side.
Go on, then. He won't be going anywhere.

speaker: hollis
lines: Fen, the owl in the pines, won't tell you anything unless you ask him. So ask him straight out.
And while you're over there, try dropping a line in the creek pool below the split pine. Just in case he dropped it in when he flew off.
Then come back and tell me what he said.

speaker: hollis
lines: You fished it out of the creek? Under the split pine?
So it wasn't Fen after all. It was the wind. Well, I never.
I suppose I'll have to say something to him. One of these days.
Here, have my spare. One mitten's no use to me on its own. And don't argue, I don't like owing anybody.

speaker: hollis
lines: The wind's picking up. Keep yourself wrapped up warm, Nana's girl.

speaker: hollis
lines: A headband? From Tamsin, the marten up in the pines? For me?
...It's a bit tight round the ears. But it stays on, and it's warm. Don't you go telling anyone I said it was warm.
Tell her it fits. And tell her she could've just asked me, you know.

speaker: bram
lines: Four hundred and... no, hang on, that one's sticking out. I'll have to start again.
Batteries? Nana sent you, did she? They're in the woodstore, behind that heap there.
The end of my pile came down, you see. Without an end the rows all lean, and I can't count a leaning row. Put it back up for me and they're yours.

choices.text: why does it need to be straight?

speaker: bram
lines: When a pile's straight, you just count the rows. When it's crooked, you have to count every single log. I've counted it three times today and got three different numbers.
And I can't go into winter with three numbers. I need the one.

speaker: bram
lines: It wants eight logs on the end, laid square across each other. And I'll know if you've cheated, because I'll count them.

speaker: bram
lines: That's still a heap. I can see it from here, you know.
Eight logs, square across each other. Then come and tell me it's done.

speaker: bram
lines: Right, let me count. Four hundred and seventy-three in the rows, and eight on the end. They're yours.
Four hundred and eighty-one. The same number twice in a row. Do you know how long it's been since that happened?
Here you are, the spare batteries. Do be careful with them, they're the only ones in the valley.

speaker: bram
lines: And since you're going up there anyway: the bridge rope on Windscar Ridge is wearing through. Everyone knows it.
Tuck, the marten who looks after that bridge, hasn't spoken to me in years. He'd never come down here and ask.
So take him my good rope. Forty feet of it, coiled, no splices. I checked it myself.
And tell Tuck I want it back the same length. I'll be measuring it.

speaker: bram
lines: Tuck's up at the bridge on Windscar Ridge. Forty feet, mind. I'll know if it comes back short.

speaker: bram
lines: It's tied on? He took it? From me?
'Still forty feet,' he says. 'Come up and measure it yourself,' he says. Well.
And what's that you've got there, with the bent bow? Give it here. That's the key to my woodshed.
I trod on it and bent it the winter we stopped talking. And he's kept it tied in his rope all this time.
Well. Come the spring, I'll walk up there with my tape measure. Somebody has to check it.

speaker: bram
lines: Four hundred and seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one. Right, from the top. Don't talk to me, I'm counting.
Wood's the one thing in this valley that stays counted. I like that about it.
People don't, mind. People keep changing their numbers on you.
Go on, then. Watch the pile on your way past.

speaker: edda
lines: A visitor, all the way up here? You've climbed a long way to look at a dead radio.
I keep the radio set here at the mast. The whole valley talks to each other through it.
Well, they did. It's run out of power, and I'm waiting on batteries from down below.
Nana Quill, down at the cabin, is seeing to it. If you see her, tell her I'm still up here.

speaker: edda
lines: You'll be Nana's Pip. I'd know that lantern anywhere. And those must be my batteries.
There, can you hear it humming? The set's warming up. But it can only reach the valley when the aurora's out.

speaker: edda
lines: Now, here's my trouble. I'm an owl, and I see the night in greys.
Three nights now I've called out on a cloud I thought was bright, and nobody down in the valley heard a thing.
Nana's camera can see green. I can't.
So if you can catch the aurora in a photograph, come and tell me the moment it's up.

speaker: edda
lines: Look north, over the shoulder of the peak. It starts off low, like a stain on the sky. Give it time to climb.
Then come straight to me. It doesn't stay out for long.

speaker: edda
lines: Then we'll wait another night. But the snow's on its way, and when it comes, the road shuts.
Look north, over the shoulder of the peak. And come straight to me when you see it.

speaker: edda
lines: The set's warm and I've got my talon on the dial. The rest is up to the sky.
Look north, over the shoulder of the peak. It's green, low down at first, and then it climbs. Get it on the camera, then come and tell me.

speaker: edda
lines: It's up? Then here we go. Come and stand by me.
Brindle Peak calling the valley. Brindle Peak calling. Is anyone there? Over.
Nothing yet, only static. The sky has to find us first. Give it a moment...
There!

speaker: bram
lines: Hearth Hollow here, by the big pine. The woodstore's full. Four hundred and eighty-one logs. Over.

speaker: orla
lines: Come up and have some, any of you. Over.

speaker: skiff
lines: The boathouse on the Frozen Reach here. The ice is holding, and the lake's nice and quiet. Over.

speaker: ivy
lines: Anyone who's cold, come on down. Over.

speaker: wren
lines: It's Wren, in Pinewind Wood. The mast's humming again, I can hear it from here. Over.

speaker: gus
lines: It's Gus, at the bell shop in the hamlet! I'm holding the big bell's rope right now!
Next time you call, I'm going to ring it. I really am. Over.

speaker: edda
lines: Can you hear that, faint, under the others? That's the road crew, down below the pass.
They're bringing the plough up in the morning. The road's staying open.

speaker: nana
lines: Edda, is that you? Is Pip up there with you?
Oh, good. Oh, that's good. No, don't tell me anything, I want to hear it from her.
And everyone along the trail, if there's a post near you, light it. She'll be coming down in the dark.

speaker: edda
lines: That's the whole valley, and the line's holding.
Thirty winters I've kept this set, and I've never heard it so crowded.
Go on home now, Pip. Follow the lights down.
I'll look after the set. Brindle Peak, over and out.

speaker: edda
lines: The line's held ever since. They've hardly stopped talking.
Bram, down by the big pine, has read me his count four times now.
Give Nana my love, would you? She'll pretend she doesn't need it.
Watch yourself on the ridge going down. The wind's in a mood tonight.
